chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
title: The Rhythm Club as a place to cut and learn
summary: McRae contrasts today's young players with the Rhythm Club on 132nd and 7th, where top musicians cut each other and Hawkins, Waller and Hines came by.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And this is what a lot of musicians today to get their experience because there was no place for them to play.
You know, they study a lot and they stay in the room. When he goes out, where can he go?
What's that club I told you where we used to have the cutting sessions? The Baby uh --
Not the Baby Grand. You know what I'm talking about. Next to that right on the corner of 132nd Street and 7th Avenue.

Rhythm Club. The Rhythm Club. Now, say for instance, they had a rhythm club where you could go out after you practice all day long -- practice in your house when you come home from work -- you want to go out.
And say you're not gigging and you're waiting for a gig, you know. And you could go out, like

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

on Thursday night or Friday night and all these top musicians are there. And they cut in with each other, telling you could get in there. Take your horn out and get in there. And you get in there and blow something with them, you know.
That'll give you an idea how you're progressing, you know. If you're studying, you know.
And that would give you an idea what you'll be up against, you know. You get an -- hear something.

I look at all the music today that's (inaudible). You know, they go to school. But if they could just get an idea -- go out in a club where maybe ten or fifteen musicians, this guy will show up. Dexter Gordon will show up, you know. Dizzy would come in, you know.
Got to be behind these guys to hear them play.
These are the things what we
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
had back there in those days, the music you don't have today.

We could rub elbows with the top men, you know. (Inaudible) walk in a place -- there's Coleman Hawkins over there, there's Louie over there, Errol Garner, Fats Waller and all those boys sitting around there.
J.P. Johnson sitting over there playing the piano. Earl Hines walk in or something like this. Hey man.
